item.title: The Healing Trap
item.description:
Trauma

The Healing Trap

Healing requires the very skills that healing is supposed to produce.

Posted August 10, 2026

Key points
  • Advice to be patient or reframe assumes capacities that distress itself often reduces.
  • Treating those capacities as prerequisites can turn a slow recovery into self-blame.
  • Small, low-stakes repetitions may build capacity that instruction alone cannot.

Anyone who has applied for a first credit card knows the shape of the problem. To be approved, you need a credit history. To build a credit history, you need to be approved. The requirement is also the outcome, and no amount of effort inside the loop breaks it.

Something structurally similar happens to people trying to recover—from bereavement, betrayal, burnout, assault, or depression. The advice is familiar and usually well meant. Be patient with yourself. Accept that change unfolds slowly. Try to see this from another angle. Trust the process.

Each of those is a capacity, not an instruction—and each is a capacity that distress tends to erode and that recovery tends to restore. We are asking people to arrive in order to travel.

Call it the healing trap.

Reappraisal Is Expensive

Cognitive reappraisal—reinterpreting a situation so that it means something less threatening—is among the better-supported strategies in the emotion regulation literature. But it is not free. It draws on working memory, attentional control, and enough distance from the feeling to turn it over.

Sheppes and colleagues gave people a choice rather than an instruction. Across three experiments using unpleasant images and unpredictable electric shock, participants tended to choose reappraisal when intensity was low and to shift toward distraction when it was high. Choosing distraction under high intensity is not a failure of nerve; it may be a sensible allocation of a limited resource. The study shows what people reach for, not what works better. But that alone is striking: One of our best-known regulation strategies may be hardest to reach for exactly when distress is greatest.

Patience may have a similar architecture, though it is rarely described this way. It can work less like a mood than an inference: Waiting gets easier when experience has given us reason to think that waiting pays. In the first weeks after a loss, that experience is precisely what is missing. Asking someone to trust that it gets better is asking for a conclusion when no premises are available.

Accepting that change unfolds unevenly is harder still. A setback in month four is information only if you already hold a model of recovery that includes setbacks. Without that model, a bad week is not a fluctuation in a trend. It is a verdict.

Why the Framing Matters

This is not a semantic quibble. When a capacity is presented as an entry requirement rather than a likely outcome, its absence stops being a description and becomes an indictment. The thought is no longer "I cannot do this yet." It is "I am failing at recovery"—a second layer of suffering stacked on the first.

That second layer may not be harmless. A meta-analysis by López-Castro and colleagues reported a moderate association between shame and posttraumatic stress symptoms. The studies are largely correlational and cannot tell us what causes what, but the pattern is consistent enough that advice that risks adding shame seems worth avoiding.

The Cosigner

The credit trap is not solved simply by trying harder. It is solved structurally, and there are two standard moves. The first is a cosigner: Someone with the standing you lack signs alongside you until you have your own.

Coan and Sbarra’s social baseline theory makes a comparable argument about regulation. Their proposal is that the human brain treats reliable social proximity as the expected condition, and that threat and effort are appraised as more costly when a trusted other is absent. The developmental version is less contested: Self-regulation emerges in the context of repeated co-regulation. Infants are soothed by others long before they can reliably soothe themselves.

So the person does not have to generate all of that patience from within. A therapist, a friend, a sibling, a group can hold it on their behalf—including the belief that this will change, which the person cannot currently generate from the inside. This is not a soft description of what support feels like. It may be a fair description of how support works.

The Secured Card

The second move is a secured card: a small limit, backed by a deposit, so that early attempts cannot fail catastrophically and every small success is recorded.

Behavioral activation runs on something like this logic. Rather than waiting for motivation to return, the person schedules modest, specific, achievable activities and does them without it. Ekers and colleagues, pooling 26 randomized trials, found behavioral activation outperformed control conditions for depression, though they noted that study quality was often low and follow-up periods short. The narrow claim worth making is this: Capacity seems more likely to be built by repetition than summoned by instruction. For someone who cannot face a whole evening out, a first attempt might be a five-minute phone call.

Practically, that means shortening the interval until the question becomes answerable. "Can I be patient about my recovery?" has no answer. "Can I get through this afternoon without issuing a verdict on myself?" does. Answer that one a few dozen times, and you have something that looks, in retrospect, a great deal like patience.

Nobody Arrives

There is a reason the destination framing is both tempting and corrosive. If healing is a place, then every day spent short of it counts as failure.

The trajectory research points elsewhere. Bonanno argued that responses to loss and potentially traumatic events follow several distinguishable paths, with a stable resilient course more common than the clinical literature once assumed. There is no single road with a finish line. The transformation stories deserve caution too: Jayawickreme and Blackie have argued that much of the evidence for posttraumatic growth rests on retrospective self-report.

If you cannot yet be patient, reframe, or trust the process, that is not evidence that you are recovering badly. It may only mean that the capacities recovery asks of you are not available to you yet. Borrow the one you are missing, and lower the limit until a first attempt is allowed to be only an attempt.

item.title: The Combination Lock: How to See Your Life as a Miracle
item.description:
Gratitude

The Combination Lock: How to See Your Life as a Miracle

Tracing the unlikley chain of events behind your blessings can deepen gratitude.

Posted August 10, 2026

Key points
  • A combination lock opens only when several numbers are entered in the exact order.
  • Many of our blessings work similarly: They exist because a sequence of events unfolded in a sparticular order.
  • Writing about the unlikely sequence of events that contributed to your blessings can deepen your gratitude.
  • This writing activity may inspire autobiographical awe and turn what seems ordinary into a miracle.

Most of us understand the danger of taking our blessings for granted. Yet simply knowing this rarely makes us grateful. Even in a life filled with good things, joy can remain strangely elusive.

So what can we do? Telling ourselves that we should be grateful is not especially helpful. Gratitude does not respond well to commands. There are simply no shoulds in gratitude.

Instead, we need to change how we understand the good things in our lives.

The Giant Combination Lock
Source: AI-generated; OpenAI/ChatGPT

The Giant Combination Lock

Think of something precious in your life as a giant combination lock. Combination locks open only when several numbers are entered in the exact order. One wrong number, and the lock remains closed.

Many of the best things in our lives work in a similar way. They exist because a long sequence of people, decisions, conversations, accidents, setbacks, and opportunities unfolded in a particular order.

Change one part of that sequence, and your life might look completely different. A friendship may have begun because you happened to attend an event you nearly skipped. A career may have emerged from a random conversation that lasted only a few minutes. A loving relationship may depend on two families making dozens of decisions across several generations.

What now feels ordinary may once have been astonishingly unlikely.

Try This Journaling Exercise

Choose one person, experience, opportunity, or circumstance in your current life that feels wonderful, precious, or meaningful. In one sentence, describe this blessing. Do not worry if you do not feel especially grateful for it right now.

Next, write down as many events as you can that contributed to this blessing becoming part of your life. Think of these events as the numbers in your giant combination lock.

Perhaps a random conversation changed the direction of your life. Maybe someone offered you encouragement at exactly the right moment. A disappointment may have redirected you toward an opportunity you would otherwise have missed. Your childhood, neighborhood, education, or family history may also have shaped what later became possible.

Use the following prompts to trace the story:

  • Which past events had to happen for this blessing to occur, and which past events increased the likelihood that it would?
  • Which seemingly minor choices or encounters helped set it in motion?
  • Who contributed to the blessing, directly or indirectly?
  • Did any disappointment or difficulty unexpectedly redirect you toward this blessing?
  • How far back can you trace the chain of events that made this blessing possible? Did you experience something in your childhood that paved the way for this blessing to occur?
  • Although the primary focus of this exercise is on past events in your life, you could also consider circumstances in your parents’ or even your grandparents’ lives. What happened in their lives that made this blessing possible?

Once you have completed your list, pause and reflect on the following:

  • Did certain events need to occur in a particular order for your blessing to occur?
  • Which past event or part of the sequence of events feels most surprising or improbable?
  • Which past event almost didn’t happen?
  • Without one of these events, how different might your life be today?
  • Who are you grateful to for helping make this blessing possible?
  • How does seeing the full sequence of events change the way you experience your blessing?

Then complete the sentence: Today, I feel grateful for...

My Own Combination Lock

I recently tried this exercise with my current job.

I have worked at the same university for almost 20 years. It is not a perfect place, and it has had its share of persistent challenges. There have been times when I have felt discouraged by circumstances connected to my work.

Still, on balance, it has been by far the best job I have ever had. I could not have asked for a more meaningful career. I have worked alongside wonderful colleagues and taught students who remind me that what I do matters.

I began listing the events that led to my being hired at the university in 2007. I thought about the people who supported my decision to pursue certain opportunities, the conversations that opened doors I could not have opened by myself, and the unusual opportunities that appeared at the right time.

Eventually, I identified at least 12 events that contributed to my getting the job. Had several of them unfolded differently, I probably would not have gotten my job at this university. For example, I got the job only because someone else turned it down.

As I traced the sequence, my job began to look different. It no longer seemed like something that had simply happened or something I was naturally entitled to possess. I saw it as the product of many people, choices, opportunities, and unlikely turns.

My heart filled with gratitude, not only for the job itself, but also for everyone who helped make it possible.

Why This Exercise Works

Here’s the problem that’s blocking your gratitude: The good things in your life become invisible when they feel inevitable. Once that happens, we begin to experience it as normal, permanent, or guaranteed.

But seeing your life’s goodness as a giant combination lock changes the status of your blessings. When you view something meaningful as the result of countless interdependent events, it becomes contingent. You recognize that it depended on prior circumstances and could easily have unfolded differently. The ordinary becomes extraordinary.

You may even begin to experience what we could call autobiographical awe: the feeling that your own life story is stranger, more fragile, and more beautiful than you had realized. You recognize that you’re part of something larger than any single moment or decision. Your life carries the fingerprints of countless people, including some you may never have met or even known about.

The next time something good in your life begins to feel ordinary, trace the combination of past events that led to it. You might discover that what seems ordinary may actually be one of the great miracles of your life.

This piece is Part 3 of a series on the narrative approach to understanding gratitude. It also appears in my Substack newsletter on the science and practice of gratitude.

item.title: The AuDHD Strength of Being Driven
item.description:
Neurodiversity

The AuDHD Strength of Being Driven

Experiencing the world through purpose and commitment with coexisting autism and ADHD.

Posted August 10, 2026

Key points
  • AuDHD drive can sustain effort long after novelty and urgency have faded.
  • Purpose can support persistence through slow progress, uncertainty, and setbacks.
  • Initiative can turn deeply held values and interests into meaningful action.

This post is the fifth and final in a five-part series exploring strengths associated with coexisting autism and ADHD. Without minimising the real challenges of AuDHD, the series draws on clinical practice and research to highlight strengths from a person-centred, strengths-based perspective. If you'd like to read the previous posts in this series, you can find them here: Part 1, Part 2, Part 3, and Part 4.

In my post, Understanding Strengths With Coexisting Autism and ADHD (Storace, 2025), I focus on interconnected strengths associated with coexisting autism and ADHD, including attuned, unified, dynamic, heartfelt, and driven. The quality of being driven reflects an enduring commitment to a purpose, goal, responsibility, or contribution. It involves the ability to focus energy, attention, and effort on what is considered worthwhile and to maintain that dedication over time.

Understanding "Driven" as a Strength

In my clinical practice, I often hear individuals with AuDHD describe two distinct forms of energy. One is the pull toward what's new, stimulating, or in motion, expressed as the dynamic strength explored earlier in this series. The other is slower-moving: the willingness to persist with one thing, one relationship, or one responsibility, long after novelty or urgency would normally keep it going. This is drive (Hallowell & Ratey, 2011). It is less about the intensity of engagement and more about its duration—the capacity to keep returning to what matters, day after day, even when nothing about the task is new or exciting anymore (Barkley, 2015).

AuDHD Drive
Source: Keith Storace

Four Dimensions of the Driven Experience

  1. Purposeful commitment: Purposeful commitment begins when a person recognises something genuinely worth pursuing and chooses to remain invested in it. Once a direction resonates, that person devotes considerable time, attention, and energy to it. Success matters less as a quick arrival at an outcome than as staying close to what holds value. The quality shows most clearly when progress is slow or uncertain. Others may become discouraged and move on. A person with a strong sense of direction persists because the work continues to hold significance.
  2. Focused contribution: Attention is rarely held for its own sake. A person who is driven directs it toward work that adds value. Whether creating, improving, understanding, supporting, or advocating, that person organises effort around making a contribution rather than completing a task. Focused contribution appears in learning, creative pursuits, advocacy, professional work, and personal development. What distinguishes it is not how intensely a person attends, but why.
  3. Resilience through purpose: Living with AuDHD means navigating misunderstanding, criticism, exclusion, and environments that do not readily accommodate different ways of thinking. Misunderstanding runs in both directions. Non-autistic people misread autistic people as often as the reverse, so what is treated as a social failing is a mismatch rather than a deficit (Milton, 2012). What distinguishes driven resilience is its shape over time: not a burst of determination in response to a single setback but a steady, low-visibility persistence that endures for months or years, unremarkable from the outside and with little external recognition. There may be no dramatic pivot or visible surge of energy, just the same determination, steadily maintained through slow progress, plateaus, or repetition, staying engaged long after something has stopped being new.
  4. Meaningful action and initiative: A person who is driven acts on an opportunity to contribute, improve, create, or advocate as soon as it comes into view. Rather than waiting for circumstances to change, that person works to shape outcomes that align with deeply held values, interests, and aspirations. Initiative of this kind goes beyond personal achievement. Over the years I have witnessed it across the education, health, and community sectors. When colleagues, students, or family members watch someone sustain that dedication, they recognise new possibilities, contribute more fully, or take up something they had set aside. Families, workplaces, and communities change because of it.
  5. Driven strength in education: Drive is expressed through a dedication to purposeful learning. Many educational systems emphasise grades, performance, and short-term outcomes, yet deep and continuing engagement emerges when students understand why their learning matters and how it connects to longer-term aspirations. Their engagement may not appear consistent from the outside. When learning feels purposeful, they demonstrate perseverance, dedication, and depth over long periods.

Students who express this strength often:

  • Commit deeply to subjects and projects they consider valuable
  • Persevere with challenging tasks because they recognise their long-term value
  • Take ownership of their learning and strive for mastery

Practical Implications for Education

When students recognise the significance of their work, they demonstrate a dedication that extends well beyond assessment requirements.

Educators can support this strength by:

  • Connecting learning to meaningful real-world applications and future possibilities
  • Providing opportunities for long-term projects that encourage sustained engagement and depth
  • Supporting student autonomy and ownership of learning
  • Recognising perseverance, dedication, and steady effort alongside academic achievement

Driven Strength in Employment

Satisfaction comes from knowing that effort contributes to something of lasting value, not merely from completing tasks or meeting external expectations. People who express this strength often:

  • See important projects through despite setbacks or periods of uncertainty
  • Maintain high standards of quality, care, and responsibility in their work
  • Take initiative when opportunities emerge to improve systems, processes, or outcomes

These qualities are most evident in workplaces that support long-term responsibility and value contributions that extend beyond immediate outcomes.

Practical Implications for Employers and Organisations

Organisations can support this strength by:

  • Communicating a clear sense of purpose, vision, and long-term direction
  • Encouraging initiative and independent thinking
  • Recognising perseverance and dedication, not only outcomes
  • Providing opportunities to take ownership of meaningful work

When these qualities are recognised and supported, those who are driven maintain momentum and advance important work.

Commitment Across Time

Purpose finds its fullest expression when effort carries it forward. Recognising the strength of being driven invites a broader view of human potential, one in which the most enduring contributions come from devoting ourselves, again and again, to what we believe is worth creating. Drive gives duration to the other four strengths of AuDHD: attunement, unification, dynamism, and heartfelt expression.

Across this series, these five strengths have described a way of engaging with the world through perception, connection, movement, sincerity, and commitment. None of this is intended to diminish the real, daily difficulties experienced by people with AuDHD, which are exhausting for many. What this series has focused on is too often overlooked: a way of flourishing in the world I continue to learn about from people with AuDHD.

item.title: Addiction Reflections and Recovery Considerations
item.description:
Addiction

Addiction Reflections and Recovery Considerations

Ongoing self-reflections, analysis, and renewal contemplations regarding addiction.

Posted August 10, 2026

Key points
  • Addiction is a complex and serious circumstance. Recovery requires acknowledgment and acceptance.
  • It is important to appreciate and understand that choices always lead to consequences.
  • Any discussion or consideration involving addiction and recovery must begin and conclude with medical advice.
Source: Moondance / Pixabay

Before making any decisions, ultimately and always, any discussion or consideration involving addiction and recovery must begin, continue, and conclude with medical advice. Addiction is a complex and serious circumstance. One point to consider is that the first step toward the road of recovery is the cognitive action of acknowledgment and acceptance (Chen, 2022; Lewis, 2018; Purje, 2014).

If acknowledgment and acceptance are not present, denial may become the determining thought, which then may continue with the ongoing addictive behavior. Without the insight of acknowledgment and acceptance of addiction, the process of recovery may not necessarily continue or even begin (Purje, 2014; Prochaska et al., 1992).

Former self-acknowledged addict Marc Lewis (a professor emeritus of developmental psychology and neuroscientist) argues that addiction is a desire, that it is learned and not a disease. According to Lewis, a behavior is often repeated when feelings of excitement, delight, or pleasure occur (Lewis, 2018).

Further to this, neuroscience informs that the neural pathways associated with repeated thoughts and behaviors become stronger and more efficient. This is the same mechanism that allows us to learn skills, form habits, or develop preferences. According to Lewis, addiction initially begins as a pattern of choices that changes the brain and leads to learned behaviors. According to Lewis, and also supported by Purje (2014), this behavior of addiction will continue until the individual makes the choice to change their thinking and behavior.

According to Lewis, this is how he eventually changed his thinking and behavior, and removed addiction from his life (which clinicians might refer to as sustained remission). Lewis’ account of addiction continues to prompt discussion, and a range of perspectives remain active in the field (Powell et al., 2026).

Disease Model vs Choice Model in Understanding Addiction

The literature informs that there are those who maintain a disease‑based interpretation of addiction, while others, including Lewis, emphasize that addiction is a choice and a developmental and learning process. These approaches reflect ongoing debates about how addiction and recovery may be thought about, understood, and explained (Lewis, 2018; Pies, 2009; Powell et al., 2026; Purje, 2014).

Cognitive behavior therapy (CBT) proposes that thoughts influence behaviors, and that learned patterns of thinking can reinforce addictive cycles. Repeated thoughts and behaviors strengthen neural pathways, and repeated thoughts reinforce cognitive potential. CBT treats addiction as a pattern of thoughts and behaviors that can be examined, challenged, and replaced. It is when this self-reflective and self-determined conscious choice and action takes place that the potential for recovery is possible (Brand et al., 2025).

Rational emotive behavior therapy (REBT) of Albert Ellis supports the requirement of self‑reflective thinking by emphasizing that individuals need to engage (in deliberate and disciplined focussed thinking), to intentionally identify and challenge their irrational beliefs that have led to their addictive behaviors. Without this intentional self-reflective cognitive engagement taking place, their irrational beliefs will remain unchallenged, and their addictive behavior will have the belief-based potential to continue. For behavior to change, beliefs must change (David et al., 2018).

William Glasser’s reality therapy emphasizes personal choice and present‑focused responsibility. The past cannot be changed. The reality of the present is the only place where changes to thinking, life, and behavior can take place (Glasser, 1965/1975). To which we add the quote from Viktor Frankl (1946/2006), who lived in unimaginable circumstances: “Between stimulus and response there is a space. In that space is our power to choose our response. In our response lies our growth and our freedom.” As such, and immutably, choices only occur in the present, and that present is now.

Another perspective worth considering is that of Stephen Yoder (2002), who argues that health and well-being are the responsibility of the individual. Yoder’s emphasis on—in the present—deliberate self-reflective decision-making and agency aligns with the cognitive and behavioral approaches (Yoder, 2002).

Further to this, Schumann and Dweck (2014) examined why some individuals accept responsibility for their actions while others do not. Their research shows that individuals who constructively and positively view themselves as capable of learning and adapting are more willing to take responsibility for their actions. This aligns with the concept that these individuals are therefore operating from an internal locus of control perspective.

Although not a clinical therapy, Responsibility Theory offers a philosophical and educational framework for understanding personal responsibility, agency and choice. The individual begins to regain the capacity to take control of their decisions, behaviours, actions and their life, which begins with the following question: “What am I responsible for, and what power do I have?” With that question posed, the answer is: “I am responsible for, and I have the power over what I think, do, say, learn and choose.” As such, a choice can change at any time and place, and with this, the intention should always be one where only positive and beneficial choices are made (Purje, 2014).

Source: Horacio Lozada / Pxabay

Ongoing Considerations

Taken together, these considerations and discussion points aim to offer insights for self-reflection and recovery. They are offered for analysis rather than prescription, the purpose of which is to allow the reader to form their own opinions and conclusions.

These frameworks present psychological models, philosophical theories, and educational perspectives, allowing individuals to consider how they choose to understand addiction and recovery and which presentation—if any—offers insight or potential. As such, and as noted, before making any decisions, ultimately, and always, any conversations or deliberations involving addiction and recovery must begin with, and continue with, medical advice.

item.title: When Trolls Come for You
item.description:
Social Media

When Trolls Come for You

The psychology of online cruelty.

Posted August 10, 2026

Key points
  • Internet trolling is meant to provoke a reaction, not to invite an honest exchange.
  • Cruel comments can activate old fears even when they come from someone who does not know us.
  • We can choose when to respond and how much access a stranger gets to our attention.

You post a photo or a comment on social media about something that matters to you. Most people scroll past it. A handful like it, and some even leave a kind comment. Then someone you’ve never met writes something mocking, cruel, or weirdly specific to the one thing you’re insecure about, and somehow that’s the comment you’re still replaying at midnight.

Source: Ralph Olazo / Unsplash

This person doesn’t know you. You can tell the comment is exaggerated, maybe a little unhinged, and written purely to get a rise out of you. It doesn’t matter. The kind comments blur together within minutes. The cruel one just sits there, lodged.

That isn’t proof that you’re too sensitive or that the troll saw something true. But knowing that doesn’t necessarily make the comment easier to forget.

Disagreement Isn’t Trolling

Somebody can push back on your idea, question your evidence, or tell you flatly that they disagree. That isn’t trolling. With trolling, the argument is mostly beside the point. The reaction is the point.

There’s actual research on this, and it’s a little grim. Trolling has been linked to psychopathy, low empathy, a desire for negative attention, and everyday sadism, or taking pleasure in another person’s distress. Everyday sadism showed the strongest association. Loneliness has also been associated with trolling, although that does not mean loneliness by itself causes someone to behave cruelly online.

These studies looked at personality traits and patterns of behavior. They do not allow us to diagnose an individual troll from a few comments. What they do help explain is why arguing back often goes nowhere. If someone is more interested in upsetting you than discussing the issue, your reaction may be what they were looking for in the first place.

Context matters, too. People often behave differently when they are anonymous and do not have to face the person they are attacking. The tone of the comment section matters as well. When hostility is already common, it becomes easier for someone else to join in.

This helps explain why someone might say things online that they would never say across a table from another person. It does not excuse the behavior. Being behind a screen may make cruelty easier, but it does not make it harmless.

Why It Gets Under Your Skin Anyway

“Don’t let it bother you” has never worked on anyone, as far as I can tell. Feelings don’t take instructions well. We’re wired to pay attention to anything that reads as a threat to our belonging, our reputation, or our safety. A public insult can hit harder than a private one for the simple reason that it happened with an audience watching, even if you have no idea whether anyone actually noticed.

Sometimes a comment lands right on an old insecurity, confirming the same negative core belief you’ve been carrying about yourself, and trying to shake, for years. As a therapist who specializes in eating disorders and body image, I’ve seen a stranger’s offhand comment about someone’s stomach, food they were excited to try, or a photo in which they felt exposed unravel weeks of progress in the span of a single scroll. The troll didn’t put that belief there, but their comment can feel like confirmation that the fear was right all along.

That is part of why “they’re just looking for attention” doesn’t help much, even when it’s true. Knowing why someone did something doesn’t undo what it did to you. Your body reacts before the calmer, more rational part of your brain gets a chance to weigh in.

It’s worse, understandably, when the comment goes after race, gender, sexuality, disability, religion, or body size. Those insults do not appear out of nowhere. They draw on stigma that existed long before the comment was typed. Telling someone to brush it off puts the burden on the wrong person.

The Pull to Defend Yourself

Source: Luke Porter / Unsplash

When someone twists what you actually said, correcting them can feel almost automatic. You think: If I just explain this clearly enough, they’ll understand. Sometimes that is true when you’re dealing with someone who is actually listening. A troll isn’t. Your explanation is exactly what they wanted. It gives them more of your attention and another opening to poke at you.

Before you type anything back, there are a few questions that may be worth asking yourself. Is this person trying to understand me, or are they trying to provoke me? If I respond, am I doing it for myself, or because I feel like I owe strangers an accurate record? What will the next hour of this cost me if I keep going?

There’s no formula that works every time. Correcting the record may feel important, especially if the comment could mislead other people. It may be worth stating a boundary. Most of the time, honestly, the strongest move is the boring one: Block, mute, report, or close the app. Refusing to argue with someone who has no interest in understanding you isn’t giving up. It’s deciding who gets access to your time.

Stalking, threats, or repeated harassment call for a different response. Save the evidence, report it to the platform, and involve law enforcement if the situation warrants it.

Taking the Meaning Back

A troll’s comment can start to feel like evidence. If they said it, maybe other people think it too. If it hurt this much, maybe it’s true. Neither of those conclusions actually follows.

Taking the meaning back starts with naming what the comment seemed to confirm. Maybe it was, I’m unattractive, I don’t know what I’m talking about, or People are laughing at me. Once you put that belief into words, you can look at where it came from and whether this stranger has any real basis for confirming it. What could the commenter realistically know about you? Usually, very little. They saw a photo, read a few sentences, or caught a small glimpse of your life. If the comment has begun to outweigh your own judgment, talk to someone who knows you well and can help you put it back in proportion.

The urge to defend yourself is normal, but you do not have to act on it. A stranger’s decision to be cruel tells you something about how they chose to behave. It does not tell you who you are.

item.title: The Holistic Psychologist and the Ethics of Psychology
item.description:
Ethics and Morality

The Holistic Psychologist and the Ethics of Psychology

Personal integrity is what we do when nobody is looking.

Posted August 10, 2026

Key points
  • A therapy license should mean the same thing whether a therapist is speaking to one person or 9 million.
  • The code of ethics we have for the consulting room says nothing about podcast studios, TikTok, or Instagram.
  • The Holistic Psychologist instructed followers to choose peace over chaos while her own household was chaotic.

Six years ago, an Esalen student showed me the PDF files she had just received for subscribing to the Holistic Psychologist's newsletter at $20 per month. To put this in context, I should confess up front that as a psychotherapist I am the worst businessperson anyone has ever met, loathing any and all marketing, never buying Google Ads, never paying for SEO stuff, and hopelessly confused about finance in general—unable to comprehend why the same person who complains about a $17 movie ticket for two hours of entertainment will gladly spend $17 for a bottle of water at the Chateau Marmont or a smoothie at Erewhon. In addition, having studied Lacan for the last 12 years, I consider my views about psychology to be somewhat subversive, but perusing the Holistic Psychologist's handouts I could see that what was being sold in those PDFs wasn't the psychology that we studied academically.

Lord Acton's statement that "Power corrupts and absolute power corrupts absolutely" seems to apply to therapists who "go viral" without having the intellectual substance to warrant such acclaim. Today, our profession affords successful practitioners a level of authority as well as power to influence not only the individuals who sit across from us in session but, thanks to social media, also "followers." Known to 9 million Instagram followers as the Holistic Psychologist, Nicole LePera has a Ph.D. in clinical psychology from the New School for Social Research and subsequently spent years telling her followers that traditional psychology shouldn't really be trusted.

This subversiveness was massively successful, racking up four New York Times bestsellers and a paid subscription base of tens of thousands of members each month. However, according to The New York Times, her most recent book "Reparenting the Inner Child" was written with a ghostwriter, even though LePera and her wife swore in legal filings that every book bearing her name had been written solely by her.

Lord Acton's insight was that scale removes the friction that normally keeps a person honest with herself. A therapist seeing 20 patients a week gets corrected constantly, by silence in the room, by a client who doesn't return, by a negative review, by a missed payment. A therapist performing to 9 million followers loses that friction and her only feedback becomes engagement numbers and book sales. The New York Times recently reported that LePera's business partners helped produce psychology content despite having absolutely no clinical training.

The platform economy has made it difficult to tell a real intellectual from a great marketer. A clinician who has sat with various psychological theories for 20 or 30 years tends to hedge, qualify herself, admit where the research contradicts itself, and always does her best to remain intellectually honest. I was suspicious of the Holistic Psychologist when I saw the two pages of PDF files she sent my student and I imagine that many of her followers will question her insights after reading the New York Times article.

What is fascinating is that the Holistic Psychologist sold transparency and radical honesty as her brand, instructed followers to recognize people who mistreat them, and choose peace over chaos, while her own household—according to dueling lawsuits replete with allegations of surveillance, misused funds, a protective order, and a physical altercation that left someone with an injured ankle—appears to have run on the chaos her books tell her followers to walk away from. Listen, we're all wounded healers, but a psychologist shouldn't build an empire on the claim that her own profession can't help people while secretly paying others to produce content in her name.

Actually, what our profession needs is a new code of ethics written for the 21st century because the code of ethics we have for the consulting room says nothing about the podcast studio, TikTok, or Instagram. A license should mean the same thing whether a therapist is speaking to one person or 9 million, and we all need to have as much personal congruence and integrity as possible. It may sound trite to articulate that therapists should practice what we preach, but until licensing boards start treating social media as clinical conduct, the field will keep creating therapists and followers who learn the hard way exactly what Lord Acton stated 150 years ago.

item.title: Don’t Talk About Your Feelings, at Least Not All the Time
item.description:
Relationships

Don’t Talk About Your Feelings, at Least Not All the Time

Relationship advice tells us to express all our feelings together. It's wrong.

Posted August 10, 2026

Key points
  • Modern relationship advice tells us to express our feelings, communicate more, and process emotions together.
  • Couples often arrive in therapy convinced that their main problem is a lack of communication.
  • The skill of self-regulation is not the same as emotional avoidance.

Many relationship experts assume that emotional disconnection sits at the heart of relationship distress. Their remedy is to turn towards each other, to reach for your partner when you’re upset or disappointed and share what’s on your mind.

It’s a modern article of faith that we should talk about our feelings and share our vulnerability. If you’re angry, say so. If you’re anxious, let your partner know. Many couples come to therapy convinced that more openness and more emotional honesty is the answer.

But what if that’s wrong and we’ve got it backwards?

Not every feeling needs an audience

Previous generations often expected relatively little emotionally from marriage. Well into the twentieth century, many marriages were emotionally restrained. Men, in particular, were expected to be guarded and emotionally reserved. Openness about feelings was uncommon and often discouraged.

A correction was overdue.

But we’ve swung too far. Now, every anxiety gets outsourced; every frustration becomes a relationship conversation. Every uncomfortable feeling is treated as something that should immediately be shared and pored over together.

If the old mistake was emotional repression, the new mistake is emotional incontinence. We have become uncomfortable with the idea that adults should be able to manage a decent chunk of their emotional lives on their own.

Self-regulation should not be confused with emotional avoidance. Some feelings need reflection. Some dissipate with time. Some are the product of hunger, exhaustion, stress or simply a bad day. Some benefit from a night’s sleep. And some can be handled on your own.

One of the most valuable relationship skills is knowing when to lean on your partner, and when not to, even if that flies in the face of the dominant messages of modern relationship advice.

The real task of a relationship: Growing up together

The central task of an intimate relationship isn't emotional fusion; it’s learning to remain connected while staying psychologically separate. It means being able to love another person without losing yourself, and being close without merging. Healthy relationships require judgement and independence, as well as openness.

In practice, that means tolerating disappointment without immediately demanding reassurance. It means accepting that someone can love you while disagreeing with you or failing to understand exactly how you feel.

Many couples expect much more. They assume a good partner should always be emotionally available, endlessly patient and ready to help them process and make sense of whatever they’re feeling, whenever they are feeling it.

But that’s an impossible job and no one can sustain it.

Your partner will sometimes be tired, distracted or preoccupied with problems of their own. They will misunderstand. They will see the world differently and they won’t always know the right thing to say. That doesn’t mean they’re emotionally unavailable; it means they’re human. And, of course, sometimes you’ll be having an unnecessarily over-the-top emotional reaction that they don’t share.

Relationships help us grow precisely because they ask us to tolerate these moments rather than eliminate them. To modern ears, that can sound cold. It isn’t. But it’s adulting — taking responsibility for your own emotional life while remaining open to love and support from another person.

The risks of emotional overdependence

The idea that you should be able to bring all of your emotional needs to your partner is so ingrained that often, if a partner struggles with that, they are cast as the problem: emotionally unavailable, avoidant or incapable of intimacy.

But being on standby to manage someone else’s emotional dependence is rarely attractive. It is difficult to sustain sexual desire for someone you feel responsible for propping up. Esther Perel has argued for years that desire requires separateness. We are attracted to people we experience as independent and capable, not people we have to look after. Love often grows through caregiving; desire does not.

The pandemic taught this lesson. Many couples had assumed their problem was that they didn’t spend enough time together or talk enough. Then COVID arrived and it turned out that wasn't the problem at all. Modern couples increasingly expect one relationship to provide what previous generations found across friends, family, neighbours, colleagues and religious communities.

Few relationships can survive that burden and the outcome is often disappointment and resentment: one partner feels overwhelmed, the other feels neglected, and both wonder where the attraction went.

The middle ground: What actually works

Good relationships depend on honesty, openness and turning towards one another. But they also depend on restraint.

Before you share something difficult, ask yourself a few questions:

  • Is this something I need to say, or just something I’m feeling right now?
  • Is this the right moment?
  • Am I looking for understanding, or am I asking my partner to make this feeling disappear?
  • Can I tolerate them seeing things differently?
  • Can I calm myself first?

Timing matters. If your partner has an important meeting tomorrow morning, put a pin in it. “Can we talk tomorrow, when I can give it my full attention?” is a reasonable request sometimes. And when you do talk, aim for acknowledgment not agreement. You don’t need your partner to tell you everything will be fine. Understanding how you feel is enough.

Recognise that people regulate themselves differently. Some people want to talk. Others would prefer to go for a run. Sometimes the healthiest response isn’t another conversation. Cook dinner together. Go for a walk. Many emotions settle without analysis.

And if you’re naturally the more emotionally expressive partner, pay attention to how often you’re looking for reassurance, validation or agreement. It feels comforting in the short term but can gradually become a dependency. And If your partner has never been emotionally expressive, don’t expect miracles. People can grow, but they rarely become someone entirely different. Loving someone means accepting their strengths and limitations.

A healthy emotional life is spread across several relationships, not concentrated in one. The goal of a relationship isn’t to narrate your inner life in real time. It’s about knowing which feelings need sharing, which need reflection and which simply need time. That’s emotional maturity.

item.title: Rescue Entitlement Dependency—Is Your Adult Child in the RED?
item.description:
Parenting

Rescue Entitlement Dependency—Is Your Adult Child in the RED?

If repeated parental rescue becomes expected, loving support becomes entitlement.

Posted August 10, 2026

Key points
  • Rescuing usually begins with love. Parents step in to ease distress, not create dependence.
  • Repeated rescue can change expectations. What starts as help can gradually come to feel owed.
  • Parents can support without rescuing. Stepping back can build confidence and independence.

Parents rarely wake up one morning and decide to make their adult child dependent on them. The process is usually much more gradual. Let's say a daughter cannot make her car payment, so her parents cover it. A son loses another job, so his father pays his car insurance. Or, suppose an adult child becomes overwhelmed by a problem, and Mom makes the phone calls, negotiates the bill, or steps in to prevent the consequences.

How Helping Gradually Starts to Feel Owed

I use the term rescue entitlement dependency (RED) to describe a relational pattern I have repeatedly observed among parents and struggling adult children. To be clear, I'm not suggesting RED is a psychiatric diagnosis. Rather, it is a descriptive framework for understanding what can happen when repeated parental rescuing becomes expected. That expectation develops into a sense of entitlement, and reliance on parental intervention becomes increasingly entrenched.

The acronym RED I use here and with my clients is intentional. Parents often rescue precisely because their adult child appears to be “in the red” financially, emotionally, vocationally, or functionally. At first, the help may be entirely appropriate. Families help one another, and there are times when an adult child genuinely needs a safety net. Yet repeated attempts to get an adult child out of the red can inadvertently create another kind of RED. That's where, if you have read any of my other posts, you may have seen me refer to parents in these situations as metaphorically acting like first responders or even SWAT team leaders.

When the Safety Net Becomes the Floor

The difficulty begins when the safety net quietly becomes part of the floor. Consider parents who begin paying their 29-year-old daughter’s rent after she loses her job. Six months later, they are still paying it. When they suggest that she begin assuming part of the expense, she responds, “You know how much I’m struggling. How can you do this to me now?” The issue is no longer simply whether she needs money. The meaning of the money has changed, and the parent-adult child relationship changes with it.

This dynamic is central to what I explore in my book, You Ruined My Life—Now You Owe Me!: How to Stop Rescuing, Reduce Conflict, and Help Your Adult Child Move Forward. Many loving parents recognize that their rescuing has gone too far, but they experience enormous guilt when they consider stepping back. I'm talking tractor-trailer loads of guilt that I hear about from my parent coaching clients. Driven by guilt (pun intended), their adult child’s distress becomes their distress, so solving the problem provides immediate relief to everyone. This feeds and shapes a sense of entitlement. Unfortunately, this is a case where the quest for immediate relief can have long-term costs.

Shifting From Rescuing to Supporting

Breaking RED does not mean becoming cold, withholding, or punitive. It means shifting from rescuing to supporting. Support communicates, “I care about what happens to you, and I will help you think this through.” Rescue too often communicates, “Your distress is unbearable to me, so I need to make the problem disappear.”

The Takeaway

Sometimes, the most empowering thing a parent can offer an adult child is not another rescue. It is the confidence conveyed by saying, “I believe you can handle more than you think you can.”

item.title: Subjective Exceptional Experiences in Self-Transformation
item.description:
Parapsychology

Subjective Exceptional Experiences in Self-Transformation

These exceptional phenomena are more common than most people think.

Posted August 10, 2026

Key points
  • Subjective reports of exceptional or anomalous experiences are common in the population.
  • Such experiences range from intense emotions to anomalous phenomena such as precognition and telepathy.
  • These experiences can be transformative, shaping self-understanding, relationships, and meaning in life.

Throughout history and across cultures, people have reported experiences that seem to transcend ordinary consciousness, traditionally interpreted as signs of divine or supernatural influence. Nonordinary states were often intentionally cultivated through ritual, trance, meditation, and communal ceremonies for healing, guidance, and insight, particularly during times of crisis. Modern research suggests that such experiences remain widespread. Large-scale surveys report subjective phenomena including precognitive dreams, meaningful coincidences or synchronicities, crisis-related telepathic impressions, and encounters with the deceased. Although individuals may subjectively experience such events only occasionally, they are broadly distributed across the population. This prevalence challenges the assumption that exceptional experiences are rare or pathological. Instead, they appear to be a relatively common dimension of human experience, worthy of psychological investigation as part of how people interpret and make meaning of their lives.

These exceptional experiences are clearly out of the ordinary and could be life-changing—that is, subjective experiences can be a gateway to self-transformation, especially when they are interpreted as meaningful within a spiritual framework. The term ‘awakening’ refers to the experience of and process leading to wakefulness as an ongoing state, described as a high-functioning mode of being in which an individual’s experience of self, social relationships, the world, and the overall existential understanding of life undergo substantial positive transformations.

To explore whether subjective exceptional experiences are linked to positive self-transformation, we conducted an online study using a representative sample of the German population. The study combined two established psychological inventories and has been made publicly available as a preprint. To assess exceptional experiences, we used the Inventory of Nonordinary Experiences, which captures a broad spectrum of subjective phenomena that stand out as markedly different from everyday experience—often described as more intense, extreme, or comprehensive than typical perceptions or states of consciousness. These include experiences that individuals themselves recognize as unusual or deeply significant.

An emotionally charged atmosphere in autumn, evoking the end of life
Source: Image by Marc Wittmann

Because such nonordinary experiences are often reported as catalysts for profound personal change, we also employed the WAKE-16 (Inventory of Secular-Spiritual Wakefulness). This measure is designed to assess forms of positive self-transformation, including increased well-being, a sense of connection, clarity of perception, and a shift in identity or life orientation. By examining how reports of exceptional experiences relate to levels of wakefulness or transformation, the study aims to understand whether and how such experiences may contribute to enduring psychological growth. In a recent Psychology Today post, I discussed the concept of “awakening” and the development of the WAKE-16 by a research team led by Steve Taylor of Leeds Beckett University. This framework provides a useful lens for interpreting the transformative potential of exceptional human experiences.

Our findings suggest that nonordinary experiences are far from rare. Overall, such subjective reports occur to a significant extent within the general population. When focusing specifically on parapsychological or anomalous experiences—such as telepathy, precognition, perceived past-life memories, or sensing the presence of unseen forces or beings—the reported frequency falls within low to moderate. Yet, when examined more closely, individual reports of these experiences range between 10 percent and 30 percent, a remarkably high prevalence that aligns with large-scale surveys conducted in other countries.

Clear differences also emerged across categories of subjective experience. Intense emotional experiences—such as profound love, joy, or grief—were reported most frequently. These were followed by experiences of psychic abilities, altered senses of self, and bodily or unusual perceptual phenomena. In contrast, experiences involving meaning, perceived presences, or health-related anomalies were less commonly endorsed. Notably, domains such as psychic abilities appear to exist along a continuum, ranging from common, widely accepted phenomena like déjà vu to rarer and more controversial reports such as extrasensory perception or past-life memories. Taken together, these findings support earlier research indicating that a substantial minority of individuals report at least some anomalous or exceptional experience, highlighting their relevance for understanding the broader landscape of human consciousness.

Importantly, the Inventory of Nonordinary Experiences emerged as a significant positive predictor of WAKE-16 scores. Individuals who reported exceptional experiences were also more likely to report higher levels of positive self-transformation—what can be described as an awakening process. Notably, the strongest association with awakening was found in the inventory item group related to meaning. Experiences such as sudden, profound insights into the nature of reality or moments in which the purpose and direction of one’s life become strikingly clear were particularly predictive of higher wakefulness scores. These findings suggest that it is not merely the occurrence of exceptional experiences that matters, but how they are interpreted and integrated. In this sense, exceptional experiences that foster clarity, coherence, and a deeper sense of meaning may serve as catalysts for positive psychological transformation. Powerful emotions play a further key role in self-transformation. Such experiences can expand an initially self-focused perspective, fostering a deeper sense of connection to others, nature, or even a higher reality.

In conclusion, our findings suggest that nonordinary experiences are a widespread and multifaceted dimension of human life, extending beyond the pathological or culturally marginal interpretations often applied to them, as Donna Thomas and Sarah Durston have argued in their book Self and Subjectivity in Social Research. Such experiences occur across the general population in diverse forms and intensities. While emotionally intense experiences—such as love, awe, joy, and grief—are most common, explicitly anomalous experiences are also reported by a substantial minority. Rather than a sharp boundary between “ordinary” and “nonordinary” experience, these findings suggest a continuum of human experience. Importantly, exceptional experiences may also contribute to meaning-making and, when constructively integrated, support lasting psychological and spiritual transformation. Studying these experiences may therefore help psychology better understand not only unusual states of consciousness, but also human potential for growth, self-transcendence, and awakening.

The Bial Foundation in Porto, Portugal supports this research. Grant number 356/24 to Cecilia Bastos and Marc Wittmann: “Exceptional experiences and stable self-transformation over time in contemplative practice."

item.title: How to Counter AI Misinformation to Children
item.description:
Artificial Intelligence

How to Counter AI Misinformation to Children

Proactive adults can educate young people about digital fabrication.

Posted August 10, 2026

Key points
  • Children's vulnerability to deceptive content is impacted by algorithmic suggestions and peers.
  • Children judge digital credibility based in part on surface cues and source familiarity.
  • To protect young users, adults can select AI content with clear labeling and decreased personalization.

In a world where artificial intelligence (AI) is becoming ubiquitous, adults are increasingly discussing its pros and cons with children. Using the technology together is another workable method of incorporating this new digital tool into family life and learning. This assimilation is more effective when parents understand the way their children already view AI platforms and capabilities. The viewpoints of children depend on their age, gender, perception skills, susceptibility to peer influence, and familiarity with the AI tool they are using.

Source: Image by Bob from Pixabay

Vulnerability to AI Misinformation

Certainly, it’s not just children who are fooled by AI-generated text and images. Yet there are areas in which children may be uniquely vulnerable. Research explains.

Md Uzzal Talukder (2026) examined the impact of AI-generated misinformation on children.[i] Recognizing the ability of AI to create highly realistic misinformation, he notes that children’s vulnerability to deceptive content is fueled in part by reliance on surface cues and limited critical literacy, exacerbated by algorithmic suggestions and sharing with peers. Noting that educational and regulatory safeguards remain works in progress, he calls for educators and caregivers to create child-centered protocols to address appropriate use of AI use in a fashion designed to account for developmental vulnerabilities.

Talukder reports that children’s susceptibility to AI-generated misinformation is based on predictable cognitive and developmental patterns. He explains that for children, especially in early and middle childhood, judgments of credibility are based on surface cues including perception, language fluency, and source familiarity. He notes that for this young audience, emotionally engaging digital content may intensify reliance on these cues, and also notes that current generative AI systems can create visuals, coherent-sounding text, and fabricated citations that seem real, or are difficult to quickly verify, particularly among younger users.

Children’s Partnerships With AI Tools

Besides the age of the child, vulnerability to AI-generated misinformation also depends on the reason children are using AI tools, both educationally and personally.

Zeynep Aydemir et al. (2026) used a sample of 521 students in Türkiye to investigate how fourth and eighth graders view artificial intelligence.[ii] Regarding general familiarity with the technology, almost all of the students reported having seen the term "artificial intelligence." Aydemir et al. found that older students described AI in more abstract and cognitively oriented ways, while most of the children associated it with technology like robots, phones, and computers. Aydemir et al. found gender differences as well. Female students endorsed empathetic and anthropomorphic representations within AI models, while male students focused on functional and technical features. Regarding how frequently the children used AI, Aydemir et al. discovered that children who used digital devices more often were more likely to view AI with more complexity, including recognizing AI’s interactive, and human-like features.

Aydemir et al. also investigated the perception of AI’s conceptual limitations, including the fact that it lacks moral judgment, emotions, creativity, and existence as an autonomous agent, which they note illustrates growing conceptual sophistication as children age.

Adult Wisdom Augments Artificial Assistance

For parents and caregivers, Talukder is one of many voices suggesting practical strategies include viewing AI-mediated content with children, as well as introducing them to credibility-testing techniques such as verifying sources. He recognizes that users and designers can also implement safety features such as clear AI labeling, and decreasing personalization efforts for content delivered to minors. He also acknowledges what many caregivers and educators seek to put into practice within their own cities and schools, that by combining efforts in education, policy, technology design, and child caregiving, adults can work together to ensure the future of AI as “a tool for empowerment rather than manipulation” in the digital lives of our precious young people.
